title: Compare two data sets on a double bar graph and answer questions

lesson.title: Two Bars, One Question

steps.say: You already know how to read a double bar graph, even when each square counts by fives or tens. Today we take one small step further: using those two bars side by side to compare and answer questions.

Here is the trick. On a double bar graph, the two colours are two different groups. To compare, you look at one label at a time and read both bars there. If you want to know how many more, you read both numbers and subtract.

visual.caption: Recycled cans collected, Class A in one colour and Class B in the other

steps.say: Let us try it with a real question. This graph shows cans two classes collected for the school recycling drive. On Monday, Class A collected twenty cans and Class B collected thirty five cans. Question one: who collected more on Monday? Class B, because thirty five is bigger than twenty. Question two: how many more? Thirty five take away twenty is fifteen more cans.

visual.caption: Monday: Class A twenty cans, Class B thirty five cans

steps.say: Here is a mistake lots of kids make. Some children see that Class B has three taller bars and say Class B is ahead by three. But three is the number of days, not the number of cans! The bars tell you cans. Always compare the numbers the bars stand for, not how many bars look taller.

Now a whole day question. On Tuesday, Class A collected twenty five cans and Class B collected thirty. Together on Tuesday that is twenty five plus thirty, which is fifty five cans. And across all three days, Class A collected twenty plus twenty five plus fifteen, which is sixty cans, while Class B collected thirty five plus thirty plus twenty, which is eighty five cans. So Class B collected twenty five more cans in total.

visual.caption: Three day totals: Class A sixty cans, Class B eighty five cans

steps.say: So the whole idea is simple. Find the label, read both bars, then compare or subtract to answer the question.

lesson.answer: Read both bars at the same label, then compare or subtract to answer.

practice.question: A double bar graph shows money raised at a Burnaby school bake sale by two grades. On Friday, Grade 5 raised forty dollars and Grade 6 raised fifty five dollars. On Saturday, Grade 5 raised sixty dollars and Grade 6 raised forty five dollars. Draw the double bar graph yourself if it helps. Which grade raised more on Friday, and by how much? Which grade raised more over the two days together, and by how much?
practice.answer: On Friday, Grade 6 raised more, by fifteen dollars, because fifty five take away forty is fifteen. Over the two days, Grade 5 raised forty plus sixty, which is one hundred dollars, and Grade 6 raised fifty five plus forty five, which is one hundred dollars too. They raised exactly the same amount, so neither grade is ahead.
